abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a unified information-theoretic framework for understanding and designing neural networks that fundamentally reconceptualizes the learning process. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on empirical risk minimization, we propose that neural network training can be equivalently understood as minimizing the mutual information between network parameters and input data while maximizing the information bottleneck principle at each layer. This paradigm shift enables us to derive theoretically optimal network architectures without relying on extensive hyperparameter tuning or empirical validation. We prove that under mild conditions, any feedforward network trained with standard gradient descent implicitly implements an information-theoretic regularization that promotes minimal sufficient representations. The framework provides rigorous bounds on the generalization error in terms of information-theoretic quantities, offering new insights into why deep networks generalize despite their enormous parameter counts. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that networks designed according to our theoretical principles achieve competitive performance while exhibiting remarkable robustness to overfitting. This work establishes a new mathematical foundation for neural network theory that bridges the gap between information theory and deep learning practice, opening avenues for principled neural architecture search and optimal network design.

We present refined generalization bounds for deep neural networks that significantly improve upon existing theoretical guarantees by incorporating data-dependent complexity measures. Previous PAC-Bayes bounds suffer from loose constants and fail to capture the implicit regularization effect of stochastic gradient descent. Our analysis introduces a novel notion of empirical trajectory complexity that characterizes the effective capacity of neural networks trained with gradient-based methods. We prove that the generalization gap can be bounded in terms of the sharpness of the loss landscape at the found minima, establishing a rigorous connection between optimization dynamics and generalization performance. The derived bounds are tighter than state-of-the-art results by a factor proportional to the network depth, providing more meaningful predictions for practical architectures. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to recurrent neural networks handling sequential data, demonstrating that the temporal unfolding structure introduces additional regularization effects that improve generalization. Experimental validation on various architectures including ResNets and LSTMs confirms that our theoretical bounds accurately track actual test error across different dataset sizes and network configurations. This work provides practitioners with theoretically grounded guidance for selecting appropriate network capacities and training hyperparameters.

We introduce Hierarchical Spiking Neural Architecture (HSNA), a novel computational paradigm that fundamentally reimagines neural network design through biologically-inspired hierarchical organization. Unlike conventional artificial neural networks that operate with synchronous, rate-based activations, HSNA employs a multi-scale temporal coding scheme where information is represented across different time scales, mimicking the temporal dynamics observed in biological neural circuits. The architecture consists of hierarchically connected spiking neuron layers with adaptive synaptic plasticity mechanisms that enable autonomous feature extraction without explicit supervision. We develop a hardware-efficient training algorithm that operates directly in the spike domain, eliminating the need for rate-based approximations or surrogate gradient methods. The proposed system demonstrates remarkable energy efficiency when implemented on neuromorphic hardware, achieving comparable accuracy to conventional deep networks while consuming orders of magnitude less power. Extensive experiments on pattern recognition tasks including image classification and speech recognition show that HSNA achieves competitive accuracy while exhibiting superior temporal processing capabilities for sequential data. The architecture naturally supports online learning and continual adaptation, making it particularly suitable for edge computing and autonomous systems operating in dynamic environments.

This paper presents Adaptive Graph Neural Architecture (AGNA), a significantly enhanced framework for graph neural networks that addresses fundamental limitations in existing architectures. While current graph neural networks rely on fixed aggregation functions that struggle with heterogeneous graph structures, AGNA introduces learnable aggregation operators that automatically adapt based on local graph topology and feature distributions. The architecture incorporates a novel message-passing mechanism with attention-weighted neighborhood sampling that maintains linear complexity while capturing long-range dependencies in large-scale graphs. We design a curriculum-based training strategy that progressively introduces more complex graph structures, enabling better convergence and improved generalization. The system includes an efficient parameter-sharing mechanism across different graph layers that substantially reduces memory footprint without compromising expressiveness. Extensive evaluation on node classification, link prediction, and graph classification benchmarks demonstrates that AGNA consistently outperforms existing graph neural network variants, achieving relative improvements of up to 15% on challenging benchmark datasets. The architecture shows particularly strong performance on graphs with varying node degrees and heterogeneous edge types, where conventional methods typically struggle. We provide an open-source implementation with optimized inference pipelines for real-world deployment.
